slides.headline: Practices, each with its reason
slides.body: Read this table as two columns: what breaks without the practice is the mirror image of the reason.

header: The reason, in terms of mechanism
rows: Small commits, one logical change each
a commit is the unit of revert, cherry-pick, bisect and review; a commit that does three things can only be undone, ported or blamed as three things
the message is the only part of a commit that records why; the diff already records what
a ref anyone can move is a ref anyone can break or rewind; a rule turns "we agreed not to" into "the server refuses"
a second reader catches what the author's model of the change hides, and spreads knowledge of the code
a check that is not required is advice; and a check must run on the merged result to mean anything about main
history is copied to every clone and fork and cannot be recalled; deleting the file adds a commit and removes nothing

header: The reason, in terms of mechanism
rows: a bare force sets the server's ref with no check; a lease makes the push conditional on the ref being where you last saw it
Signed commits and tags where identity matters
author and committer fields are text that anyone can set; a signature is evidence that a key holder made the object
rules, workflow triggers and cleanup scripts select branches by pattern
rebasing rewrites commit IDs; on a branch nobody else has, nobody else can be holding the old IDs
No history rewriting on shared branches
everyone who fetched the old commits now has a history that diverges from the server, and the next careless merge brings the removed commits back
a merge brings every commit reachable from the other side, not only the ones you had in mind

slides.headline: Anti-patterns, each with its root cause
slides.body: An anti-pattern is rarely stupidity.

header: Root cause: the model behind it
rows: "a commit is a save point for my day", not a unit of change
stage by hunk (git add -p); one logical change per commit
"the repository is private", or "I will delete it in the next commit"
rotate first, then clean up; push protection
"everything needed to run should be in the repository", confusing sources with outputs
ignore outputs; commit the inputs and the lock file
"rebase tidies history", without the fact that it creates new commits
rebase only what nobody else has; merge on shared branches
"the push was rejected, so force it": the rejection is read as an obstacle and not as information
read the rejection; fetch; --force-with-lease --force-if-includes; forbid force pushes on shared branches by rule

header: Root cause: the model behind it
rows: know the three trees; git stash or commit first
"merging a branch brings my change", not "everything reachable from it"
make checks required; fix or delete flaky tests; know why CI differs from your machine
a tutorial from before 13 August 2021, when GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations; or one long-lived token with full scope shared by a team
"Git stores my project", without the fact that every clone carries every version of every file
"it is on GitHub, so it is backed up and it is the truth"
label the layer: which behavior is Git's, which is the platform's

slides.headline: Step 8: your configuration
slides.body: Replay labs/run ref/professional-config and show the file again.

lines.s: # ~/.gitconfig: personal Git configuration, checked on Git 2.55.0.
useConfigOnly = true # refuse to guess an identity
defaultBranch = main # unconfigured Git 2.55 still creates master
ff = only # never integrate by accident
autoSetupRemote = true # first push sets the upstream
prune = true # forget branches deleted on the server
conflictStyle = zdiff3 # show the common ancestor in conflicts
autoSquash = true # fixup! commits find their place
updateRefs = true # stacked branches move together
missingCommitsCheck = error # a deleted todo line stops the rebase
auto = 0 # avoid the MERGE_RR.lock race of Git 2.55
algorithm = histogram # moved code reads as a move
autocorrect = prompt # show the suggestion, run nothing
bareRepository = explicit # the planned Git 3.0 default
credentialsInUrl = die # refuse a token inside a remote URL
path = ~/.gitconfig-work # last, so that it wins inside ~/work/

Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Defending a rule with "best practice". Root cause: the mechanism that pays for the rule was never stated, so the rule has no defense when it costs time.
Enforcing the convention and forgetting the truth. Root cause: a linter checks the form of a message, and form does not make a message true.
Squash-merging large pull requests. Root cause: the squash makes the pull request the unit of undo, so one mistake can only be reverted together with everything else.
Treating "Request changes" or CODEOWNERS as enforcement. Root cause: review is a practice; only a ruleset turns it into a condition the server checks.
Reporting a squash-merged branch as abandoned work. Root cause: commit-based checks test ancestry and patch identity, and a squash keeps the content while discarding both.

beats.text: Commit message conventions. The subject line says what the commit does, the body says why, and trailers carry facts that tools read.
beats.tele: Commit message conventions. The subject line says what the commit does, the body says why, and trailers carry facts that tools read.

beats.text: Git itself imposes one piece of structure: the first line, up to the first blank line, is the subject, which is what git log --oneline, git shortlog and git format-patch use. Everything else is convention.
beats.tele: Git itself imposes one piece of structure: the first line, up to the first blank line, is the subject, which is what `git log --oneline`, `git shortlog` and `git format-patch` use. Everything else is convention.

beats.text: The most cited one is Chris Beams's seven rules: separate subject from body with a blank line. Limit the subject to about 50 characters. Capitalize it. Don't end it with a period. Use the imperative mood. Wrap the body at 72 characters. Use the body to explain what and why, not how.
beats.tele: The most cited one is Chris Beams's seven rules: separate subject from body with a blank line. Limit the subject to about 50 characters. Capitalize it. Don't end it with a period. Use the imperative mood. Wrap the body at 72 characters. Use the body to explain what and why, not how.

beats.text: Try it now, for thirty seconds. In any repository of yours, type git log --oneline --graph -6. It only reads. For each of the six subjects, ask one question: would a stranger know what this commit does? I'll wait.

beats.text: If one of them says wip or fix, you're in good company. Almost every history has some. And you know the cost now: the message is the only part of a commit that records why.
beats.tele: If one of them says `wip` or `fix`, you're in good company. Almost every history has some. And you know the cost now: the message is the only part of a commit that records why.

beats.text: Conventional Commits 1.0.0 adds a machine-readable prefix: type, optional scope, a colon, a description. fix corresponds to a PATCH release in Semantic Versioning, feat to a MINOR one, and a BREAKING CHANGE footer, or an exclamation mark after the type, to a MAJOR one. Other types such as docs or chore are allowed. The point is that release tooling can compute the next version number and a changelog from the history.
beats.tele: Conventional Commits 1.0.0 adds a machine-readable prefix: type, optional scope, a colon, a description. `fix` corresponds to a PATCH release in Semantic Versioning, `feat` to a MINOR one, and a `BREAKING CHANGE` footer, or an exclamation mark after the type, to a MAJOR one. Other types such as `docs` or `chore` are allowed. The point is that release tooling can compute the next version number and a changelog from the history.

beats.text: Trailers are lines of the form Key: value at the end of the message: Co-authored-by, Signed-off-by, which git commit -s adds, Reviewed-by, or an issue reference. git interpret-trailers parses them, and git log --format='%(trailers:key=Co-authored-by)' prints them.
beats.tele: Trailers are lines of the form `Key: value` at the end of the message: `Co-authored-by`, `Signed-off-by`, which `git commit -s` adds, `Reviewed-by`, or an issue reference. `git interpret-trailers` parses them, and `git log --format='%(trailers:key=Co-authored-by)'` prints them.

beats.text: What the convention cannot do. It doesn't make a message true. fix: typo on a commit that changes a rate limit passes every commit-message linter. A convention is enforced the same way as any other local check: a commit-msg hook for fast feedback, and a required check or the squash-merge title for the guarantee.
beats.tele: What the convention cannot do. It doesn't make a message true. `fix: typo` on a commit that changes a rate limit passes every commit-message linter. A convention is enforced the same way as any other local check: a `commit-msg` hook for fast feedback, and a required check or the squash-merge title for the guarantee.

beats.text: A picture helps. Think of each practice as an insurance policy with a named risk. If you can name the risk and the day it pays out, the policy survives a budget discussion. If you cannot, it's cancelled the first time money is short.
beats.tele: A picture helps. Think of each practice as an insurance policy with a named risk. If you can name the risk and the day it pays out, the policy survives a budget discussion. If you cannot, it's cancelled the first time money is short.

beats.text: Small commits pay out on the day of a revert, a backport or a bisect. A protected main pays out on the day somebody's push would have rewound it. The message pays out the day somebody asks why a line exists and the author has left.

beats.text: Where the picture breaks: an insurance policy costs the same whether or not you understand it, and a practice does not. A team that follows a rule without its reason follows it badly: commits that are small in lines and still mix three changes, messages that satisfy the linter and say nothing.

beats.text: Squash-merging large pull requests. Root cause: the squash makes the pull request the unit of undo, so one mistake can only be reverted together with everything else.

beats.text: Treating "Request changes" or CODEOWNERS as enforcement. Root cause: review is a practice; only a ruleset turns it into a condition the server checks.
